chunks: Muhammad (ibn al-Hassan) narrated from al-Fadl, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
I asked him: 'Does a man blow (air) in prayer at the place of his forehead?' He said, 'No.'
Muhammad ibn al-Hassan said: This report is to be understood as indicating dislike (karahah), based on the evidence of the reports we have previously mentioned.

key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَةِ: dislike (a legal ruling less severe than prohibition)
key_terms.مَوْضِعَ جَبْهَتِهِ: at the place of his forehead

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on blowing air at the forehead during Islamic prayer?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the ruling on blowing air at the forehead during prayer, with the jurist Muhammad ibn al-Hasan interpreting the negative response as indicating *karahah* (dislike) rather than strict prohibition (*haram*). This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly method of reconciling seemingly contradictory narrations to establish nuanced legal rulings within the chapter on prayer etiquette. The practice is thus viewed as a recommended act of refinement rather than a mandatory or forbidden one, reflecting the balance between ritual purity and personal comfort in Shia fiqh.
